beats.intro: Chapter one. [[sub]]Demand and supply. How sensitive buyers are to price, why extra workers add less and less, and when a firm should keep producing.
beats.demand: [[line]]Start with demand. When the price of a good rises, buyers choose to buy less. That is the law of demand. [[eq]]For one household's gasoline, a demand function says: quantity equals fifty-seven, minus six point three nine times the price. [[p1]]At one euro forty-eight a liter, the household buys about forty-seven and a half liters a month. [[p2]]Raise the price by one euro, and it buys about six point four liters fewer.
beats.elas: [[f]]How sensitive is quantity to price? The slope depends on units: liters or gallons, euros or dollars. So economists use elasticity: the percentage change in quantity demanded, divided by the percentage change in price. [[ex]]If price rises ten percent and quantity falls eight percent, elasticity is negative zero point eight. [[unit]]Percentages carry no units, so the answer is the same in any currency and any measure.
beats.slide: [[a]]Elasticity changes along a straight demand curve. [[p1]]Here the price is low, one forty-eight, and elasticity is only about negative zero point two. Demand is inelastic: quantity barely responds. [[slide1]]Slide up the curve. [[unit]]At about four forty-six, elasticity is exactly negative one. Unit elastic. [[slide2]]Higher still, elasticity grows beyond one in size. Demand is elastic: buyers react strongly.
beats.spend: [[r]]Now add total expenditure: price times quantity, the green rectangle. [[down]]Move the price back down. While demand is elastic, a lower price raises spending. [[peak]]At unit elasticity, spending peaks. [[low]]Below that, demand is inelastic, and cutting the price lowers spending. [[rule]]So whether a price change raises or lowers spending depends on elasticity.
beats.income: [[a]]The same idea works for other variables. Income elasticity is the percentage change in quantity demanded, divided by the percentage change in income. [[pos]]Positive means a normal good: more income, more purchases. [[neg]]Negative means an inferior good: more income, fewer purchases. [[b]]Cross-price elasticity uses the price of a different good. [[sub]]Positive means substitutes: when tea gets dearer, people buy more coffee. [[comp]]Negative means complements: when cars get dearer, people drive less and buy less gasoline. [[ex]]In our example, income elasticity is about plus point two six, and cross-price elasticity with cars is about negative point eight four.
beats.effects: [[a]]When the price of a good falls, two things happen. [[se]]The substitution effect: the good is now cheaper than its alternatives, so you buy more of it. [[ie]]The income effect: your money stretches further, as if you were richer. [[norm]]For a normal good, both push the same way, so quantity rises a lot. [[inf]]For an inferior good, the income effect pulls the other way, but the substitution effect still wins, so quantity rises by less. [[giff]]In the rare Giffen case, the income effect wins, and a lower price means less demanded.
beats.returns: [[a]]Now the supply side. Add workers to a fixed factory. [[b1]]The first worker adds twelve units. [[b2]]The second adds ten. [[b3]]The third, eight. [[b4]]Then six, [[b5]]four, [[b6]]and two. [[c]]This is diminishing marginal returns: with some inputs fixed, each extra unit of a variable input adds less than the one before. [[tot]]Total output still grows, to forty-two, but more and more slowly.
beats.costs: [[a]]A firm's costs come in two kinds. Fixed cost does not change with output. Variable cost does. [[avc]]Divide variable cost by output, and you get average variable cost. [[mc]]Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit. It first falls, then rises, because of diminishing returns, and it cuts through the average curves at their lowest points. [[atc]]Average total cost adds average fixed cost on top. That extra gap shrinks as output grows, so the curve is U-shaped.
beats.profit: [[a]]A firm that takes the market price produces where price equals marginal cost. [[hi]]At a high price, it earns a profit: price is above average total cost. [[be]]At about eleven point nine, price equals the lowest point of average total cost. That is the breakeven point. [[loss]]Below it, the firm loses money. But as long as price covers average variable cost, producing still helps pay the fixed costs. [[sd]]Below about six, price cannot even cover variable cost. That is the shutdown point. The firm should stop producing.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Elasticity is a percentage change in quantity divided by a percentage change in something else, so it has no units. [[w2]]Demand elasticity decides whether a price change raises or lowers total spending. [[w3]]Normal goods, inferior goods, substitutes and complements are told apart by signs. [[w4]]Diminishing returns shape the cost curves, and price against average costs tells you when to produce, break even or shut down.
